_comment: Bundled Messier deep-sky catalog (J2000). Static data file, no network. Coordinates are accurate to a fraction of a degree — enough for observability ranking (altitude/transit/window), which is what the night planner uses them for. Sourced from the standard Messier catalog. Fields: id, name (common name or ''), ra_deg, dec_deg, type, con (constellation abbrev), size_arcmin (optional major-axis angular size in arcminutes, for the 'will it fit in one frame?' framing hint; omitted when not vetted).; size_minor_arcmin (optional minor-axis angular size in arcminutes, vetted for the objects bigger than one Seestar frame, so the 'how big a mosaic?' panel-count plan knows an elongated object needs fewer panels than its major axis alone implies; omitted when not vetted); distance_ly (optional distance in light-years, for the 'how far did you see?' light-travel line; the renderer rounds hard, so these are the standard published figures and need no more precision than that; omitted when not vetted); blurb (optional beginner-friendly one-liner about the object, shown on the 'what am I looking at?' card; omitted when not curated)

objects.name: Crab Nebula
objects.blurb: The wreckage of a star seen to explode in 1054 AD, bright enough that astronomers around the world recorded it. It still glows about 6,500 light-years away in Taurus.
A dense ball of well over a hundred thousand ancient stars in Aquarius, and one of the richest globular clusters in the sky. Its core stays a soft glow even in a good scope.
One of the finest globular clusters in the northern sky, packed with hundreds of thousands of old stars. A spring favourite, riding high in Canes Venatici.

objects.name: Cat's Eye Cluster
objects.blurb: One of the closest globular clusters to us, a loose ball of ancient stars near the bright orange star Antares in Scorpius. Easy to resolve into a sparkle of individual suns.
A big, bright globular cluster in Serpens and one of the oldest known — its stars are thought to be around 13 billion years old, nearly as old as the universe.

objects.name: Butterfly Cluster
objects.blurb: A bright scatter of young stars in the tail of Scorpius, whose brightest members trace the outline of a butterfly with its wings open.

objects.name: Ptolemy Cluster
objects.blurb: A big, loose cluster in Scorpius, bright enough that Ptolemy noted it in the second century. It spans more than two full Moons, so give it a wide field.

objects.name: Lagoon Nebula
objects.blurb: A huge, bright star-forming cloud in Sagittarius — one of the showpiece nebulae of the summer Milky Way.
A modest globular cluster in Ophiuchus, sitting close to the dark dust lanes near the centre of our galaxy — dust that dims its light on the way to us.
One of the closer globular clusters to us, a rich ball of old stars in Ophiuchus that breaks into pinpoints with a little aperture.

objects.name: Wild Duck Cluster
objects.blurb: A rich, compact swarm of hundreds of stars in Scutum, set against the glow of the Milky Way. Named for a flight of ducks its brightest stars seem to trace.
A looser, more open globular cluster in Ophiuchus, and a near neighbour of M10 in both sky position and distance — an easy pair to shoot in one session.

objects.name: Hercules Cluster
objects.blurb: The finest globular cluster in the northern sky: a tight ball of several hundred thousand ancient stars, about 22,000 light-years away.
A rich but distant globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It never quite resolves in a small scope, staying a smooth, grainy ball of light.
One of the most tightly packed globular clusters known — its core has collapsed into an extraordinarily dense knot of stars. Easy to find in Pegasus.

objects.name: Eagle Nebula
objects.blurb: A star-forming nebula famous for the towering 'Pillars of Creation' at its heart, made iconic by the Hubble Space Telescope.

objects.name: Omega Nebula
objects.blurb: A bright emission nebula in Sagittarius, also known as the Swan or Checkmark Nebula for its distinctive shape.
A small, sparse group of young stars in Sagittarius, tucked between the Omega Nebula and the great Sagittarius star cloud.
A noticeably oval globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It lies close to the centre of our galaxy, whose gravity is thought to have stretched it out of shape.

objects.name: Trifid Nebula
objects.blurb: A striking star-forming region that pairs pink emission gas with blue reflection nebulosity, split into lobes by dark dust lanes.
A compact knot of young, hot stars in Sagittarius, right next door to the Trifid Nebula — the two sit comfortably together in a single frame.

objects.name: Sagittarius Cluster
objects.blurb: One of the brightest globular clusters in the sky, a dense ball of hundreds of thousands of stars in Sagittarius. Big and bright — a rewarding, easy target when it clears the horizon.
A rich, wide scatter of well over a hundred stars in Sagittarius, set against the crowded star fields of the summer Milky Way.

objects.name: Sagittarius Star Cloud
objects.blurb: Not a cluster but a window: a gap in the dust that lets you look straight through to a distant arm of the Milky Way, thick with stars.
A bright, loose cluster in Sagittarius, easy in binoculars and a pleasant wide-field target on a summer night.
A small, modest cluster in Scutum, usually passed over for its dazzling neighbour M11 — worth a look for the curious sparse gap near its centre.

objects.name: Dumbbell Nebula
objects.blurb: A bright planetary nebula — the glowing shell of gas cast off by a dying Sun-like star, and one of the easiest planetaries to image.
A compact globular cluster in Sagittarius, sitting close in the sky to the bright star at the top of the Teapot.
A small, boxy group of hot young stars in Cygnus. Dust between us and it hides much of its true brilliance.
A compact globular cluster in Capricornus whose core has collapsed, leaving a very dense centre with streamers of stars running outward.

objects.name: Andromeda Galaxy
objects.blurb: The nearest large spiral galaxy to our own, about 2.5 million light-years away — the most distant object most people can see with the naked eye.
A small elliptical galaxy that orbits the giant Andromeda Galaxy, often caught in the same frame.

objects.name: Triangulum Galaxy
objects.blurb: A large face-on spiral galaxy in our Local Group, roughly 2.7 million light-years away — rewarding but faint.
A bright, loose cluster in Perseus, spread over an area wider than the full Moon — a lovely wide-field target on an autumn night.
A big, bright cluster of several hundred stars at the feet of Gemini, with the much smaller, far more distant cluster NGC 2158 tucked beside it.
A young cluster of hot blue stars in Auriga — the smallest and youngest of the three bright clusters strung along that constellation.
The richest of Auriga's three clusters: a dense sprinkle of several hundred stars, with a distinctly orange one near the middle.
A loose cluster in Auriga whose brighter stars are often said to trace a crooked cross. The small cluster NGC 1907 sits close by.
A big, sparse triangle of bright stars in Cygnus, close enough to us that it spreads across about the width of the full Moon.

objects.name: Winnecke 4
objects.blurb: A curiosity rather than a showpiece — Messier catalogued a nebula here, but there is only a close pair of stars in Ursa Major.
A bright, easy cluster just below Sirius, with several orange giants scattered among its white stars.

objects.name: Orion Nebula
objects.blurb: The brightest nebula in the sky and a vast stellar nursery about 1,340 light-years away — the classic first target for almost every beginner.

objects.name: De Mairan's Nebula
objects.blurb: A bright knot of the Orion Nebula, separated from the main cloud by a dark lane of dust.

objects.name: Beehive Cluster
objects.blurb: A bright, sprawling open cluster in Cancer, visible to the naked eye as a hazy patch since ancient times.

objects.name: Pleiades
objects.blurb: The Seven Sisters: a young, brilliant open cluster wrapped in wisps of blue reflection nebulosity, about 440 light-years away.
A rich, even cluster in Puppis with a small planetary nebula apparently sitting inside it — a chance line-up, as the nebula is much closer to us.
A bright, coarse cluster of hot young stars in Puppis, close enough to show as a naked-eye smudge from a dark site. The richer M46 sits beside it.
A large, bright cluster in Hydra, spread across an area wider than the full Moon and an easy catch in binoculars.
A giant elliptical galaxy in the heart of the Virgo cluster — a smooth, featureless ball of hundreds of billions of old stars.
A pretty, heart-shaped cluster in Monoceros, set in the rich Milky Way fields between Sirius and Procyon.

objects.name: Whirlpool Galaxy
objects.blurb: A textbook face-on spiral caught interacting with a smaller companion galaxy — its grand spiral arms are a favourite target.

objects.name: Scorpion Cluster
objects.blurb: A pretty, star-rich open cluster in Cassiopeia, easy to find and up most of the year from northern skies. Sits near the small, glowing Bubble Nebula.
A compact globular cluster in Coma Berenices, far out in our galaxy's halo and one of the more distant globulars Messier listed.
The most distant globular cluster in Messier's list, and not really ours at all — it belongs to a small galaxy our own is slowly pulling apart.
A large, loose globular cluster low in Sagittarius. Its stars are spread out enough that even a modest scope resolves them.
A small, modest globular cluster in Lyra, set in a rich Milky Way field between Albireo and the Ring Nebula.

objects.name: Ring Nebula
objects.blurb: A small, bright planetary nebula in Lyra shaped like a smoke ring — the glowing shell of a dying star.
A barred spiral galaxy in the Virgo cluster, and one of the brighter spirals in a region otherwise dominated by featureless ellipticals.
An elliptical galaxy in the Virgo cluster, noticeably elongated, and often framed together with its bigger neighbour M60.
A big elliptical galaxy at the eastern edge of the Virgo cluster, with a small spiral galaxy that appears to be touching its edge.
A face-on barred spiral in the Virgo cluster and one of its larger members — a good target for showing off spiral arms.
A lopsided globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It passes close to the centre of our galaxy, which has tugged one side of it out of shape.

objects.name: Sunflower Galaxy
objects.blurb: A bright spiral galaxy whose many tightly-wound, patchy arms give it a flower-like look.

objects.name: Black Eye Galaxy
objects.blurb: A spiral galaxy with a dramatic dark band of dust across its bright core, giving it a 'black eye'.
A spiral galaxy seen at a steep angle in Leo, and one of the Leo Triplet — M65, M66 and NGC 3628 all fit together in a single frame.
The brightest member of the Leo Triplet, a spiral galaxy whose arms are visibly lopsided after a past brush with its neighbours.
One of the oldest open clusters known — most such clusters scatter long before this one has. Its stars are roughly the same age as the Sun.
A globular cluster in Hydra, sitting well below the plane of our galaxy in the sparse outer halo.
A small, compact globular cluster in the base of the Sagittarius Teapot, and one of the closest to our galaxy's centre.
A compact globular cluster in Sagittarius, near-twin to M69 close by — an easy pair to catch in one session.
A loose, sparse globular cluster in the little constellation Sagitta — so open that astronomers argued for years over whether it was a globular at all.
A faint, distant globular cluster in Aquarius, lying far out on the other side of our galaxy's centre from us.
Four faint stars in a small Y-shape in Aquarius, with nothing linking them but our line of sight — a genuine oddity in the catalogue.

objects.name: Phantom Galaxy
objects.blurb: A beautiful but faint face-on 'grand-design' spiral — a rewarding challenge under dark skies.
A small but remarkably dense globular cluster in Sagittarius, and one of the most distant Messier catalogued.

objects.name: Little Dumbbell Nebula
objects.blurb: A small planetary nebula, a fainter cousin of the Dumbbell, shaped like a cork or peanut.

objects.name: Cetus A
objects.blurb: A barred spiral in Cetus with an exceptionally bright core, powered by a supermassive black hole feeding at its centre.
One of the brightest reflection nebulae in the sky — dust glowing blue by the light of young stars in Orion.
An unusual globular cluster in Lepus, on the far side of the sky from our galaxy's centre — and probably not born here at all, but captured from a passing dwarf galaxy.
A compact, richly concentrated globular cluster in Scorpius, sitting midway between Antares and the head of the scorpion.

objects.name: Bode's Galaxy
objects.blurb: A bright, well-shaped spiral galaxy in Ursa Major, often imaged alongside its neighbour the Cigar Galaxy (M82).

objects.name: Cigar Galaxy
objects.blurb: An edge-on 'starburst' galaxy erupting with new stars, its centre torn by reddish filaments of glowing hydrogen.

objects.name: Southern Pinwheel Galaxy
objects.blurb: A bright, face-on barred spiral galaxy — a southern-sky showpiece full of pink star-forming regions.
A giant elliptical galaxy in the heart of the Virgo cluster, and one end of Markarian's Chain — a curving line of galaxies that fits in one wide frame.
A smooth, lens-shaped galaxy at the northern edge of the Virgo cluster, in Coma Berenices.
A giant elliptical galaxy beside M84 in Markarian's Chain, and unusual for moving toward us rather than away as it plunges through the Virgo cluster.

objects.name: Virgo A
objects.blurb: A giant elliptical galaxy at the heart of the Virgo cluster, home to the first black hole ever directly imaged.
A neat, many-armed spiral galaxy in the Virgo cluster, tilted about halfway between face-on and edge-on.
An almost perfectly round elliptical galaxy in the Virgo cluster — one of the roundest known.
A large spiral galaxy in the Virgo cluster whose star-forming gas is being stripped away as it moves through the crowded cluster.
A barred spiral in the Virgo cluster and the faintest object in Messier's list — it was considered lost for nearly two centuries before being identified again.
A rich globular cluster in Hercules — often overlooked next to its famous neighbour M13, but splendid in its own right.
A compact, wedge-shaped cluster of a few dozen bright stars in Puppis, low in the southern winter sky.
A bright spiral galaxy in Canes Venatici with a glowing ring of newly born stars around its core, and a much fainter outer ring beyond that.
A barred spiral in Leo whose arms curl into a near-perfect ring around the bar — a textbook example of the type.
The brightest galaxy of the Leo I group, a spiral with slightly asymmetric arms, sitting close in the sky to M95 and M105.

objects.name: Owl Nebula
objects.blurb: A round planetary nebula whose two dark 'eyes' give it an owl-like face.
A dusty spiral galaxy seen almost edge-on in Coma Berenices — one of the Virgo cluster's near-side members.
A face-on spiral in the Virgo cluster with one arm pulled noticeably out of shape, probably by a close pass with a neighbour.
One of the biggest and brightest spiral galaxies in the Virgo cluster, seen face-on with two prominent arms.

objects.name: Pinwheel Galaxy
objects.blurb: A large, face-on spiral galaxy with sweeping arms — bright core, but the faint arms reward long integration.

objects.name: Spindle Galaxy
objects.blurb: A lens-shaped galaxy in Draco seen nearly edge-on and cut by a sharp dark dust lane. Which object Messier meant by this entry was argued over for two centuries.
A small, fan-shaped cluster in Cassiopeia, and one of the last entries in Messier's own published list.

objects.name: Sombrero Galaxy
objects.blurb: An edge-on spiral with a bright bulge and a sharp dark dust lane, giving it the look of a wide-brimmed hat.
A compact elliptical galaxy in Leo that shares a frame with two fainter neighbours — a tidy little group for one night's shooting.
A bright spiral galaxy in Canes Venatici with an active core powered by a supermassive black hole.
A loose globular cluster in Ophiuchus, unusual for the dark dust patches that appear to cross its face.

objects.name: Surfboard Galaxy
objects.blurb: A long, mottled edge-on galaxy in Ursa Major, near the Owl Nebula.
A barred spiral in Ursa Major, just below the bowl star Phecda — close enough to that bright star that its glare is worth keeping out of frame.
The second dwarf companion of the Andromeda Galaxy, a soft elliptical glow in the same wide field.
